items.criterion: The pseudo-depth method estimates relative target depth from 2D images by measuring the distance from the bounding box bottom to the image bottom edge. It relies on two scene priors: the camera is above ground and all objects lie on a flat plane. Pseudo-depth reflects the occlusion order, with closer objects having larger values, enabling depth-based scene decomposition without 3D sensors.

Beyond reproducing DCM and sweeping depth levels and thresholds, the report provides significantly deeper mechanistic analysis than the original paper by introducing random-partition and reverse-order (far-to-near) controls, quantifying the exact trade-off between candidate sparsification and boundary-induced splitting of true pairs, and demonstrating a pairwise relative depth-gating alternative that eliminates greedy boundary errors in extreme crowds.
items.criterion: Depth Cascade Matching (DCM) uses pseudo-depth to partition trajectories and detections into multiple depth levels. It performs IoU-based association sequentially from the nearest to the farthest depth level, propagating unmatched objects to deeper levels. This hierarchical decomposition transforms dense crowds into sparse subsets, reducing association ambiguity and improving occlusion handling.

items.criterion: SparseTrack integrates pseudo-depth and DCM into the tracking-by-detection pipeline, achieving state-of-the-art results on MOT17, MOT20, and DanceTrack using only IoU matching. It substantially outperforms the IoU-only baseline ByteTrack (e.g., +2.0 HOTA, +0.7 MOTA on MOT17). The number of depth levels for low-score detections is critical: increasing levels improves association of occluded targets up to an optimum (4–6 levels), after which gains saturate. DCM is plug-and-play and can enhance existing trackers, demonstrating that depth-based target decomposition is a powerful strategy for dense occlusion tracking.
